metadata.title: Heights and the specialization map for Families of elliptic curves over $\PP^n$

extraction_notes.note: Theorem B is stated twice in identical unnumbered theoremB environments (Introduction and Section 5); only the Section 5 copy, the one followed by the proof, got a node, since neither is numbered and the wording is equally full.

The Introduction's setup (K, E/K minimal, reduction hom, specialization map) is restated in Sections 3 and 5; one node per notion was kept (K from the intro, E/K and sigma_t from the later fuller copies).

Section 4 'Proof of Theorem A' is a proof argued in prose with no proof environment; the whole section body is taken as the proof node, with the intermediate claim about B_P kept as steps rather than a separate claim.

Sentences that both introduce notation (I_f, E_0(K)) and invoke a cited result (codimension of indeterminacy/Pic isomorphism; reduction homomorphism from Silverman AEC) were typed as external theorem and definition respectively.
The author's earlier result [WWP] on average height ratios is stated in prose; typed as an external theorem rather than a remark because it is a cited result stated in full.
Not extracted: the roadmap paragraph, the convention that varieties are irreducible, the motivational sentence before Lemma 6, and the acknowledgements environment.

nodes.name: Function field K of P^n
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 2$, let $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(T_1, \ldots, T_n)$ be the function field of the projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.
nodes.genus: function field of the projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$

nodes.name: Canonical height on E(K)
nodes.statement: Let $O$  be the zero element of $E(K)$ and $\hat{h}_E$ be the canonical height on $E(K)$ corresponded to the divisor $(O)$.

nodes.name: Canonical height on the reduction E_Gamma
nodes.statement: Similarly, we denote $O_\Gamma$ to be the zero element of $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ and $\hat{h}_{E_\Gamma}$ to be the canonical height on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ corresponded to the divisor $(O_\Gamma)$.
nodes.statement_short: $O_\Gamma$ is the zero of $E_\Gamma$ and $\hat h_{E_\Gamma}$ the canonical height for the divisor $(O_\Gamma)$.

nodes.name: Theorem A
nodes.statement:
Given any $P \in E(K)$, there exists a set $B_P$ consisting of a finite number of codimension-two subvarieties in $\mathbb{P}^n$, such that if $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$ and $E_\Gamma/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$ is non-singular, then
$$\frac{\hat{h}_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}= \hat{h}_E(P). $$
nodes.statement_short: For almost all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma$ (avoiding finitely many codim-2 subvarieties), $\hat h_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)/\deg\Gamma=\hat h_E(P)$.
assumptions: Given any $P \in E(K)$
$\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$ and $E_\Gamma/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$ is non-singular
conclusions: there exists a set $B_P$ consisting of a finite number of codimension-two subvarieties in $\mathbb{P}^n$

nodes.name: Néron's specialization theorem
nodes.statement: In the setting of general abelian varieties over $K=k(\mathbb{P}^n)$ for any number field $k$, N\'eron (\cite{NPA}) proved that there are infinitely many $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(k)$ such that $\sigma_t$ is injective.
assumptions: general abelian varieties over $K=k(\mathbb{P}^n)$ for any number field $k$
conclusions: there are infinitely many $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(k)$ such that $\sigma_t$ is injective

nodes.name: Masser's specialization theorem
nodes.statement: Later, Masser (\cite{MSF}) proved a stronger result in a more general setting of abelian varieties $A$ defined over $K=k(V)$, the function field of a projective variety $V$ defined over a number field $k$. Masser proved that the specialization map $\sigma_t$ is ``almost always'' injective by showing that the set of $t \in V(k)$ with Weil height bounded by $h$ and such that $\sigma_t$ is not injective lies on a hypersurface of degree bounded by a constant power of $h$.
nodes.statement_short: For abelian varieties over $k(V)$, non-injective specializations of Weil height $\le h$ lie on a hypersurface of degree polynomial in $h$.
assumptions: abelian varieties $A$ defined over $K=k(V)$, the function field of a projective variety $V$ defined over a number field $k$
conclusions: the set of $t \in V(k)$ with Weil height bounded by $h$ and such that $\sigma_t$ is not injective lies on a hypersurface of degree bounded by a constant power of $h$

nodes.name: Silverman's Theorem C (injectivity off bounded height)
nodes.statement: Moreover, in the case where $V=C$ is a smooth curve, Silverman (\cite{SHS}, Theorem C) proved that the set of $t \in C(\overline{k})$ for which $\sigma_t$ is not injective is a set of bounded height.
assumptions: $V=C$ is a smooth curve
conclusions: the set of $t \in C(\overline{k})$ for which $\sigma_t$ is not injective is a set of bounded height

nodes.name: Normalized Weil height h_C on a curve
nodes.statement: There is a Weil height $h_{C,\phi}$ (that depends on the closed embedding of $\phi : C \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^m$) on $C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ and we normalize it to $h_C:=h_{C,\phi}/\deg \phi$.

nodes.name: Silverman's specialization theorem (Theorem B of [SHS])
nodes.statement:
Silverman (\cite{SHS}, Theorem B) proved that for $\pi : A\longrightarrow C$, a family of abelian varieties over a smooth curve, we have
$$\lim_{\substack{t \in  C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \\ h_{C}(t) \rightarrow \infty} }   \frac{\hat{h}_{A_{t}}(P_{t})}{h_{C}(t)} = \hat{h}_{A_\eta}(P_\eta), $$ where $A_\eta/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(C)$ is the generic fiber of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: For a family of abelian varieties over a curve, $\hat h_{A_t}(P_t)/h_C(t)\to\hat h_{A_\eta}(P_\eta)$ as $h_C(t)\to\infty$.
assumptions: $\pi : A\longrightarrow C$, a family of abelian varieties over a smooth curve

nodes.name: Comparison of Theorem A with Silverman's theorem
nodes.statement: Our Theorem A is analogous to the elliptic surface version of Silverman's theorem despite the fact that there's no limit involved and we view $\deg \Gamma$ as the Weil height of $\Gamma$. The main reason for this difference is the type of global field over which the reduction  $E_\Gamma$ is defined: over a curve $C$, $\Gamma=\{t\}$ is a point and $E_t$ is an elliptic curve over a number field, whereas over $\mathbb{P}^n$ for $n \geq 2$, $E_{\Gamma}$ is an elliptic curve over a function field. Consequently, the canonical height $\hat{h}_{E_{t}}$ on $E_{t}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ is derived from a Weil height in a number field and the canonical height $\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}$ on $E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ is derived from  a Weil height in a function field. As we shall see in section \ref{lemma}, the theory of Weil heights over the function field of a smooth hypersurface is related to the intersection theory of divisors in the projective space, i.e. B\'ezout's theorem and this is where the degree of $\Gamma$ comes into play.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem A has no limit, unlike Silverman's theorem, because $E_\Gamma$ lives over a function field where heights reduce to intersection theory (Bézout), making $\deg\Gamma$ the height of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Average of specialized height ratios over P^n (Wong)
nodes.statement: Thus, the author studied instead the average value of the quotient $\hat{h}_{E_{t}}(P_t)/h_{\mathbb{P}^n}(t)$ over rational $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{Q})$ with bounded height. As the bound tends to infinity, the author showed that this average remains finite and uniformly bounded below by a nonzero constant for all non-torsion $P$ in $E(\mathbb{Q}(\mathbb{P}^n))$.
nodes.statement_short: The average of $\hat h_{E_t}(P_t)/h(t)$ over rational $t$ of bounded height stays finite and bounded below by a positive constant for non-torsion $P$.
assumptions: rational $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{Q})$ with bounded height
non-torsion $P$ in $E(\mathbb{Q}(\mathbb{P}^n))$
conclusions: this average remains finite and uniformly bounded below by a nonzero constant

nodes.name: Convergence of the average height ratio
nodes.statement: Even in this simple case of $\mathbb{P}^n$ with $n\geq 2$, it is still an open question whether this average converges, let alone whether it converges to $\hat{h}_{E}(P)$.

nodes.name: Smooth projective variety V over k
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a smooth projective variety defined over a number field $k$.

nodes.name: Degree map deg_phi on divisors
nodes.statement: We fix a closed embedding $\phi : V \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^n$ and thus the degree map $\deg_\phi$ is well-defined on $\operatorname{Div}_{\bar{k}}(V)$, i.e. for any prime divisor $D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\bar{k}}(V)$, $\deg_\phi (D)$ is the degree of the projective subvariety $\phi(D)$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$ and we extend it linearly to all divisors.

nodes.name: Weil height over a function field
nodes.statement:
For any $P=[f_0: \ldots: f_r]$ in $\mathbb{P}^r(\bar{k}(V))$, the Weil height of $P$ is given by
$$h_{\mathbb{P}^r(\bar{k}(V))}(P):= \sum_{\Gamma} \max_i\{-\operatorname{ord}_{\Gamma}(f_i)\}\deg_\phi(\Gamma), $$ where the summation is taken over all prime divisors in $\operatorname{Div}_{\bar{k}}(V)$.
nodes.statement_short: $h(P)=\sum_\Gamma \max_i\{-\mathrm{ord}_\Gamma f_i\}\deg_\phi\Gamma$ over prime divisors of $V$.

nodes.name: Geometric interpretation of the Weil height (Lang)
nodes.statement:
(Lang \cite{LFD} Chapter 3, Proposition 3.2 ) Let $V$ be a projective variety in $\mathbb{P}^n$, non-singular in codimension one, defined over a number field $k$, and let $P$ be a point in the projective space $\mathbb{P}^r$, rational over $k(V)$. Let $f_P:V \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r$ be the rational map defined over $k$, determined by $P$. Then
$$h_{\mathbb{P}^r(\bar{k}(V))}(P)=\deg f_P^{-1}(L) $$for any hyperplane $L$ of $\mathbb{P}^r$, such that $ f_P^{-1}(L)$ is defined, the degree being that in the given projective embedding of $V$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: The function-field Weil height of $P$ equals the degree of the pull-back of a hyperplane under the rational map $f_P$.
assumptions: $V$ be a projective variety in $\mathbb{P}^n$, non-singular in codimension one, defined over a number field $k$
$P$ be a point in the projective space $\mathbb{P}^r$, rational over $k(V)$
conclusions: $$h_{\mathbb{P}^r(\bar{k}(V))}(P)=\deg f_P^{-1}(L) $$for any hyperplane $L$ of $\mathbb{P}^r$, such that $ f_P^{-1}(L)$ is defined
nodes.label: LH

nodes.name: Elliptic curve E over k(V)
nodes.statement: Let $E/k(V)$ be an elliptic curve over the function field $k(V)$ defined by a Weierstrass equation and $O$ be the zero element.
nodes.genus: elliptic curve over the function field $k(V)$

nodes.name: Weil height h_E on an elliptic curve
nodes.statement:
Then this embedding of $E$ into $\mathbb{P}^2_{k(V)}$ is induced by the very ample divisor $3(O)$. Let $h_E$ be the Weil height corresponds to this embedding, i.e. for any $P=[x:y:z] \in E(k(V))$, 
$$h_E(P)=h_{\mathbb{P}^2(k(V))}([x:y:z]). $$

nodes.name: Canonical height on an elliptic curve over k(V)
nodes.statement:
Since the divisor $3(O)$ is even, the canonical height $\hat{h}_E$ induced by $(O)$ is defined by
$$\hat{h}_{E}(P):=\frac{1}{3}\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\frac{h_{E}([n]P)}{n^2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\hat h_E(P)=\frac13\lim_n h_E([n]P)/n^2$.

nodes.name: Homogeneous coordinates S_i
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 2$ and $S_0, \ldots, S_n$ be the homogeneous coordinate functions of the projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

nodes.name: Infinity hyperplane H_infinity
nodes.statement: If we denote $T_1:=\frac{S_1}{S_0}, \ldots, T_n:=\frac{S_n}{S_0}$, then $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(T_1, \ldots, T_n)$ and the infinity hyperplane $H_\infty$ is the plane defined by $S_0=0$ .

nodes.name: Elliptic curve E/K with minimal Weierstrass equation
nodes.statement:
Let $E/K$ be an elliptic curve defined by the Weierstrass equation 
\begin{equation} Y^2Z=X^3+AXZ^2+BZ^3 \end{equation} with $A,B \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[T_1, \ldots, T_n]$ such that it is minimal with respect to all prime divisors in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that are not $H_\infty$, i.e. $$0\leq \operatorname{ord}_D(A) <4 \qquad \text{or}\qquad  0\leq \operatorname{ord}_D(B)<6  $$  for all prime divisors $D \neq H_\infty$.
differentia: minimal with respect to all prime divisors in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that are not $H_\infty$
nodes.statement_short: $E/K: Y^2Z=X^3+AXZ^2+BZ^3$ with polynomial $A,B$, minimal away from $H_\infty$.

nodes.name: Weierstrass equation of E
nodes.statement: Y^2Z=X^3+AXZ^2+BZ^3
nodes.label: WE

nodes.name: Discriminant Delta_E
nodes.statement:
The discriminant 
$$\Delta_E=-16(4A^3+27B^2) $$ is a non-zero element in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[T_1, \ldots, T_n]$.

nodes.name: Local ring O_Gamma at a hypersurface
nodes.statement: For any smooth hypersurface (smooth irreducible codimension-one subvariety) $\Gamma$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$, the local ring at $\Gamma$ is a discrete valuation ring ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ with maximal ideal $\frak{m}_\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Reduction map f -> f_Gamma
nodes.statement: We denote the reduction map ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma \longrightarrow {\mathcal O}_\Gamma/\frak{m}_\Gamma= \overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$ by $f \longmapsto f_\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Reduction E_Gamma of E modulo Gamma
nodes.statement:
Then for $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$, the reduction of $E$ modulo $\Gamma$, $E_\Gamma$ is the cubic curve (possibly singular) over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$ defined by 
$$Y^2Z=X^3+A_\Gamma XZ^2+B_\Gamma Z^3,$$ as $A,B \in {\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ for all $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$.

nodes.name: E_0(K) and the reduction homomorphism P -> P_Gamma
nodes.statement:
Let 
$$E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))_{\text{ns}}:=\{ \text{ non-singular points of }E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))\} $$ and
$$E_0(K)=\{ P \in E(K) \ | \ P_\Gamma \in E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))_{\text{ns}}\}, $$
then we have a group homomorphism (\cite{SAE} Chapter VII, Proposition 2.1. Note: the condition that $K$ is complete in Proposition 2.1 is only needed to prove the surjectivity of the reduction map, which is not needed here.)
\begin{align*}
E_0(K) &\longrightarrow E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))_{\text{ns}} \\
P=[x:y:z] &\longmapsto P_\Gamma=[x_\Gamma: y_\Gamma: z_\Gamma],
\end{align*} where at least one of $x,y,z \in {\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ is not in $\frak{m}_\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: $E_0(K)$ = points reducing to non-singular points of $E_\Gamma$; reduction $P\mapsto P_\Gamma$ is a homomorphism on it (Silverman AEC VII.2.1).

nodes.name: Codimension of the indeterminacy locus and Pic isomorphism
nodes.statement:
In general, if we have a rational map $f : V \dashrightarrow W$ between projective varieties and $V$ is non-singular, the indeterminacy locus of $f$, which we denote as $I_f$, has codimension at least $2$ (\cite{SAT} Chapter III, Proposition 3.5b) and so we have the following isomorphism (\cite{HAG} Chapter II, Proposition 6.5b) of divisor class groups induced by the inclusion $j:U:= V\backslash I_f \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow V$:
\begin{align*}
j^*: \operatorname{Pic}(V) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(U)\\
c &\longmapsto  c \cap U
\end{align*}with projective closure in $V$ as the inverse homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: For $V$ non-singular, the indeterminacy locus $I_f$ has codimension $\ge2$, so restriction $\mathrm{Pic}(V)\to\mathrm{Pic}(V\setminus I_f)$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: a rational map $f : V \dashrightarrow W$ between projective varieties and $V$ is non-singular
conclusions: the indeterminacy locus of $f$, which we denote as $I_f$, has codimension at least $2$

nodes.name: Pull-back f^{-1} of divisor classes under a rational map
nodes.statement_short: $f^{-1}:\mathrm{Pic}(W)\to\mathrm{Pic}(V)$ is pull-back along $f|_U$ followed by the inverse of restriction to $U=V\setminus I_f$.

nodes.name: Pull-back commutes with restriction to a hypersurface
nodes.statement:
For $n\geq 2$, let $f : \mathbb{P}^n \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r$ be a rational map and $\Gamma \stackrel{\iota}{\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}^n$ be a smooth hypersurface, where all the varieties are defined over an algebraically closed field $k$. Suppose $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f$, then 
$$(f \circ \iota)^{-1}(c)=\iota^*(f^{-1}(c)), $$ for any divisor class $c \in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb{P}^r)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\Gamma$ avoids the codim-2 components of $I_f$, then $(f\circ\iota)^{-1}=\iota^*\circ f^{-1}$ on $\mathrm{Pic}(\mathbb{P}^r)$.
assumptions: $f : \mathbb{P}^n \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r$ be a rational map
$\Gamma \stackrel{\iota}{\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}^n$ be a smooth hypersurface
Suppose $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f$
nodes.label: Le1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the complements of the indeterminacy locus, where Pic is unchanged, and use functoriality of pull-backs.

nodes.name: Weil height identity for reduction modulo Gamma
nodes.statement:
Let $f_P : \mathbb{P}^n \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^2$ be the rational map induced by $P \in E(K)$ with indeterminacy locus $I_{f_P}$. If $\Gamma \stackrel{\iota}{\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}^n$ is a smooth hypersurface such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular and $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_P}$, then 
\begin{equation}\frac{h_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}= h_E(P). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular and $\Gamma$ avoids the codim-2 components of $I_{f_P}$, then $h_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)=\deg\Gamma\cdot h_E(P)$.
assumptions: $f_P : \mathbb{P}^n \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^2$ be the rational map induced by $P \in E(K)$ with indeterminacy locus $I_{f_P}$

$\Gamma \stackrel{\iota}{\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}^n$ is a smooth hypersurface such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular and $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_P}$
nodes.label: leh

nodes.name: Weil height identity (E1)
nodes.statement: \frac{h_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}= h_E(P).
nodes.label: E1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement_short: Express both heights as degrees of pulled-back hyperplane classes (Proposition 1), commute via Lemma 2, then apply Bézout.

nodes.name: Doubling commutes with specialization
nodes.statement: For $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty$ such that the specialized point $P_t:=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is a non-singular point on the specialized (possibly singular) cubic curve $E_t$ defined by \begin{equation} Y^2Z=X^3+A(t)XZ^2+B(t)Z^3, \end{equation} $([2]P)_t=f_{[2]P}(t)$ is also well-defined and $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.
nodes.statement_short: If $P_t$ is a non-singular point of the specialized cubic $E_t$, then $([2]P)_t$ is defined and equals $[2]P_t$.
assumptions: $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty$ such that the specialized point $P_t:=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is a non-singular point on the specialized (possibly singular) cubic curve $E_t$
nodes.label: DL

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement:
For $E/K$ defined by the Weierstrass equation $(\ref{WE})$ with $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where $x,y,z \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[S_0,\ldots,S_n]$, the doubling formula (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, page 324) is
\begin{align}&[2]P=\notag \\*
&[2yz\left(\left(3x^2+Az^2\right)^2-2xz(2y)^2\right): \notag \\
&-\left(3x^2+Az^2\right)^3+z(2y)^2\left(8x^3+2Axz^2-Bz^3-y^2z\right): \notag \\
&8y^3z^3]. \end{align}
By substituting the relation $x^3=y^2z-Axz^2-Bz^3$ into the first two coordinates and then factor away the common factor $z^2$, we also have
\begin{align}&[2]P=\notag \\
&[2y\left(xy^2-3Ax^2z-9Bxz^2+A^2z^3\right): \notag \\
&4y^2\left(7y^2-6Axz-9Bz^2\right)-\left(27(y^2-Axz-Bz^2)^2+27Ax^4+9A^2x^2z^2+A^3z^4\right): \notag \\
&8y^3z]. \end{align}
Since by assumption $t\in\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty$ such that $P_t=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is defined and is a non-singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$, so $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ cannot be both zero. It is clear that $f_{[2]P}$ is defined when both $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ are not zero. When $y(t)=0$, then $3x(t)^2+A(t)z(t)^2$ is not zero or otherwise $P_t$ is a singular point on $E_t$. So formula $(\ref{D1})$ gives $([2]P)_t=[0:1:0]$, which is not a surprise as $P_t=[x(t):0:z(t)]$ is always a 2-torsion point with the given Weierstrass equation (\ref{WEt}). When $z(t)=0$, then $x(t)=0$ and $y(t) \neq 0$, since $P_t$ is a point on $E_t$. Formula $(\ref{D2})$ gives $([2]P)_t=[0:y(t)^4:0]=[0:1:0]$. Thus the induced rational map $f_{[2]P}$ is defined at such $t$. Lastly, formulae $(\ref{D1})$ and $(\ref{D2})$ are the same (with $A,B$ replaced by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$) doubling formula on the cubic curve $E_t$, so $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Use two forms of the doubling formula and check by cases ($y(t)=0$, $z(t)=0$) that $f_{[2]P}$ is defined at $t$.

nodes.name: Doubling formula (D1)
nodes.statement:
&[2]P=\notag \\*
&[2yz\left(\left(3x^2+Az^2\right)^2-2xz(2y)^2\right): \notag \\
&-\left(3x^2+Az^2\right)^3+z(2y)^2\left(8x^3+2Axz^2-Bz^3-y^2z\right): \notag \\
&8y^3z^3].
nodes.label: D1

nodes.name: Reduced doubling formula (D2)
nodes.statement:
&[2]P=\notag \\
&[2y\left(xy^2-3Ax^2z-9Bxz^2+A^2z^3\right): \notag \\
&4y^2\left(7y^2-6Axz-9Bz^2\right)-\left(27(y^2-Axz-Bz^2)^2+27Ax^4+9A^2x^2z^2+A^3z^4\right): \notag \\
&8y^3z].
nodes.label: D2

nodes.name: Multiples avoiding singular reduction
nodes.statement: With the minimality of the Weierstrass equation that defines $E/K$, for any $P \in E(K)$, there exists a natural number $N$ such that $([N]P)_\Gamma$ is not a singular point on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Some multiple $[N]P$ reduces to a non-singular point modulo every smooth hypersurface $\Gamma\neq H_\infty$.
assumptions: the minimality of the Weierstrass equation that defines $E/K$
for any $P \in E(K)$
conclusions: there exists a natural number $N$ such that $([N]P)_\Gamma$ is not a singular point on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$
nodes.label: LNS

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: For any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma$, its local ring ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ is a DVR with fraction field $K$ and residue field $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$, which is a perfect field.  With the minimality assumption on the Weierstrass equation, $E/K$ is defined by a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ and minimal with respect to the prime divisor $\Gamma$. Thus, the smooth part of the Weierstrass model gives the N\'eron model of $E/K$ and the quotient group $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, Corollary 9.2d). So there exists $n_\Gamma \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $([n_\Gamma]P)_\Gamma$ is not a singular point on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$. Since $E_\Gamma/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$ is singular if and only if $\Gamma$ is a component of the discriminant locus and there are only finitely many such components $\Gamma_1, \ldots, \Gamma_\ell$. So $N:=\operatorname{lcm}\{n_{\Gamma_1}, \dots, n_{\Gamma_\ell}\}$ will satisfy the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Finiteness of $E(K)/E_0(K)$ from the Néron model at each of the finitely many bad hypersurfaces; take the lcm.

nodes.name: Twisted curve E' with no pole at H_infinity
nodes.statement:
Let $k:=\max\left\{ \left\lceil \frac{\deg A}{4}\right\rceil, \left\lceil \frac{\deg B}{6}\right\rceil \right\}$ and 
\begin{equation} E'/K: \qquad  Y^2Z=X^3+\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{4k}AXZ^2+\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{6k}BZ^3,
\end{equation}
which is the elliptic curve obtained from $E/K$ by the group isomorphism 
\begin{align*} E/K &\stackrel{\approx}{\longrightarrow} E'/K \\
P=[x:y:z] &\longmapsto P'=[x':y':z']:=\left[\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{2k}x: \left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{3k}y:z \right].
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $E'$ is the $K$-isomorphic twist of $E$ by $(S_0/S_1)$ with $k=\max(\lceil\deg A/4\rceil,\lceil\deg B/6\rceil)$, and $P\mapsto P'$ the isomorphism.

nodes.name: Weierstrass equation of E' (WE')
nodes.statement: E'/K: \qquad  Y^2Z=X^3+\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{4k}AXZ^2+\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{6k}BZ^3,
nodes.label: WE'

nodes.name: Hyperplane H'_infinity
nodes.statement: The choice of $k$ is to make sure the Weierstrass equation $(\ref{WE'})$ is still minimal with respect to all prime divisors except at the hyperplane $H'_\infty$ defined by $S_1=0$.

nodes.name: Indeterminacy of f_P on H_infinity
nodes.statement_short: At $t\in H_\infty\setminus H'_\infty$ where $f_P$ is undefined, either $f_{P'}$ is undefined or $P'_t$ is singular or 2-torsion on $E'_t$.
assumptions: $t=[0,1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that the rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t$
conclusions: $P'_t$ is a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.
nodes.label: PL

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement:
If we write $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where the homogeneous polynomials $x,y,z \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[S_0, \ldots, S_n]$ have no common irreducible factor, then the induced rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ if and only if $x(t)=y(t)=z(t)=0$, because $f_P$ maps from $\mathbb{P}^n$ and so there's no way to alter it. The corresponding point $P'$ is $[S_0^{2k}S_1^kx: S_0^{3k}y: S_1^{3k}z]$. Since at least one of $x,y,z$ has no $S_0$ as its factor, we consider all possible cases:

Case 1: $z$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. Then the only possible irreducible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx$, $S_0^{3k}y$, $S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_1$ and even if we factor out this common factor, the induced rational map $f_{P'}$ is still not defined at $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*]$.  

Case 2: $y$  doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. In this case, the only possible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ are $S_1$ and $S_0$. After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$. Since $y(t)=0$ and the only possible factor we factor away from $y$ in $ S_0^{3k}y$ is $S_1$, thus $y''(t)=0$. Also, $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ by assumption. If $P'_t$ is well-defined, then it is a point on the cubic curve $E_t'(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with zero $Y$-coordinate, which implies $P'_t$ is either a singular point or a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.

Case 3: $x$  doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. The highest power of $S_0$ that can be a common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_0^{2k}$.  After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$, then we see that $y''$ always has $S_0^k$ as a factor. Thus $y''(t)=0$ and the argument follows as Case 2.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on which coordinate of $P$ is not divisible by $S_0$, tracking common factors of the coordinates of $P'$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A
nodes.statement:
Now, we put ourselves in the setting described in Section \ref{lemma}. From Lemma \ref{leh}, if $\Gamma$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^m]P}$ for infinitely many $m$, then equality (\ref{E1}) holds for these $[2^m]P$ and thus dividing equation (\ref{E1}) by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the  limit $m\rightarrow \infty$ over all $m$ such that equality (\ref{E1}) holds will give us the equality in Theorem A. A priori, such $\Gamma$ might have to avoid containing infinitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\mathbb{P}^n$ corresponding to the infinitely many rational maps $f_{[2^m]P}$, we will prove that this is not a problem. In fact, we will prove that besides finitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that might be common components of the indeterminacy locus of all $f_{[2^m]P}$, $m \in \mathbb{N}$, other  codimension-two components of the indeterminacy locus of a particular $f_{[2^m]P}$ will never reappear as components of the indeterminacy locus of  $f_{[2^\ell]P}$ for any $\ell > m$.

Since the canonical height is a quadratic form, we may replace $P$ by $[N]P$ in Theorem A. Given any $P \in E(K)$, we replace $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $\ref{LNS}$ to assure that $P_\Gamma$ is not a singular point of $E_\Gamma$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$. So if we let $S_P$ be the set of all $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that the specialized point $P_t$ is a singular point on the specialized fiber $E_t$, then $S_P$ is an algebraic set (since singularity is an algebraic property) of codimension at least two in $\mathbb{P}^n\backslash H_\infty$. In addition, we note that $S_P$ is contained in the discriminant locus $\Delta_E=0$. Similarly, we may assume the same for the corresponding point $P'$ on the isomorphic curve $E'$ defined by equation $(\ref{WE'})$, i.e. $P'_\Gamma$ is not a singular point of $E'_\Gamma$  for all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma \neq H'_\infty$ and $S_{P'}$ has codimension at least $2$ in $\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.


As before, let $I_{f_P}$ be the indeterminacy locus of the rational map $f_P$ induced by $P$. Then for all $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ that are not in $I_{f_P} \cup S_P$, $f_P(t)=P_t$ is well-defined and is not a singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$. By lemma \ref{DL} and induction on $m$, $f_{[2^m]P}(t)=\left( [2^m]P\right)_t=[2^m]P_t$ is well-defined for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Thus, $$I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap \left(\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \right) \subset I_{f_P}\cup S_P, \qquad\text{ for all }m \in \mathbb{N}.$$ The exact same argument works for $P'$ and so we also have $$I_{f_{[2^m]P'}} \cap \left(\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \right) \subset I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}\qquad\text{ for all } m \in \mathbb{N}.$$

For $$t=[0:1:*: \dots:*] \in \left(I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\right) \backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}),$$ if $t \not \in  I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}$, then lemma \ref{DL} says that $f_{[2^m]P'}(t)=([2^m]P')_t$ is defined and non-singular on $E'_t$ because $([2^m]P')_t=[2^m]P'_t$. In particular, lemma \ref{PL} implies that in fact $[2^m]P'$ is a point of order $2$ on $E'_t$. Thus, for $\ell > m$, $([2^\ell]P')_t=[2^\ell]P'_t=[2^{\ell-m}]\left([2^m]P'_t\right)=O_{E'_t}$, which implies that $t$ is not in $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ by the contrapositive statement of lemma \ref{PL}. Notice that we are left with $t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\cap H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, which is an algebraic set of codimension at least $2$ in $\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$. To summarize, we have shown that given $P\in E(K)$, by replacing $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $\ref{LNS}$ if necessary, so that $P_\Gamma$ and $P'_\Gamma$ are not singular points of $E_\Gamma$ and $E'_\Gamma$ respectively for all smooth hypersurface $\Gamma$, for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, if 
$$
  t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  t \notin I_{f_P} \cup I_{f_{P'}} \cup S_P \cup S_{P'} \cup (H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\cap H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})),
$$
then for any $\ell>m$, $t \not \in I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$. In particular, if we let
$$B_P:=\left\{ H_\infty\cap H'_\infty, \ \text{dimension-$(n-2)$ components of }I_{f_P}\cup I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_P\cup S_{P'}   \right\}, $$then for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, if $C$ is a dimension-$(n-2)$ component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ that is not in $B_P$, then $C$ is not a component of  $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ for all $\ell > m$. 

To complete the proof for Theorem A, we consider any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ that is not a component of the discriminant locus, so $E_\Gamma$ is an elliptic curve over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$. Furthermore, if $\Gamma$ does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$, then we have just shown that $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ for all big enough $m \in \mathbb{N}$. So by lemma \ref{leh}, we have $$\frac{h_{E_\Gamma}([2^m]P_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}=\frac{h_{E_\Gamma}(\left([2^m]P\right)_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}= h_E([2^m]P) $$ for all big enough $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Dividing this equation by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the limit $m\rightarrow \infty$ will give us Theorem A.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3 to $[2^m]P$, divide by $3\cdot 4^m$ and let $m\to\infty$. The key step: outside a finite set $B_P$, codim-2 indeterminacy components of $f_{[2^m]P}$ never recur for larger $m$ (Lemmas 4-6).

nodes.name: Abelian scheme over U
nodes.statement: $E/K$ is the generic fiber of an abelian scheme $\pi : {\mathcal E} \longrightarrow U$, for some Zariski open dense subset $U \subset \mathbb{P}^n$.

nodes.name: Specialization map sigma_t
nodes.statement:
Then for all $t \in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, the specialization map
\begin{align*}
\sigma_t : E(K) &\longrightarrow E_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \\
P &\longmapsto P_t
\end{align*} is a group homomorphism (\cite{SLM} Chapter 11, page 152).

nodes.name: Theorem B
nodes.statement:
Given any integer $d \geq 1$, there exist infinitely many smooth curves $C/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that do not lie in the complement of $U$ and such that the set 
$$\{ t \in C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \cap U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \ | \ \sigma_t \text{ is not injective }\} $$
is a set of bounded height. Furthermore, the union of all such curves is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: For each degree $d$, infinitely many smooth degree-$d$ curves $C\subset\mathbb{P}^n$ have $\sigma_t$ injective for $t\in C$ off a set of bounded height; their union is Zariski dense.
assumptions: Given any integer $d \geq 1$
conclusions: there exist infinitely many smooth curves $C/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that do not lie in the complement of $U$ and such that the set $$\{ t \in C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \cap U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \ | \ \sigma_t \text{ is not injective }\} $$ is a set of bounded height
the union of all such curves is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem B
nodes.statement:
If the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6) is non-zero, then by the constraint of dimension, the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is a dimensional one abelian variety, i.e. $E$ is $K$-isomorphic to $E_0 \times_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} K$ for an elliptic curve $E_0/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. So there is a Zariski dense open subset $U^0 \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ such that for all $t \in U^0(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, the fibers $E_t$ are isomorphic to $E_0$, thus the specialization maps for $\sigma_t: E_0 \times_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} K \longrightarrow E_t$  are injective for all $t \in U^0(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$. So in particular, any curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ of degree $d$ that does not lie in the complement of $U^0$ will satisfies Theorem B and their union is $\mathbb{P}^n$.

We now suppose that the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is zero, which implies that $E(K)$ is finitely generated, a result due to Lang-N\'eron (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 2). For any non-zero $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$, the algebraic set
$$ \{ t \in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\ | \ [x(t):y(t):z(t)]=\sigma_t(P)=O=[0:1:0] \}$$ has dimension at most $n-1$. Since the subgroup of torsion points $E(K)_{\text{tors}}$ is finite, so we may shrink $U$ by discarding finitely many subvarieties of dimension at most $n-1$ and assume that 
$$E(K)_{\text{tors}} \longrightarrow E_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) $$
is injective for all $t \in  U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$. On the other hand, We will use the canonical height pairing to prove that the specialization map is injective on the free part of $E(K)$. The canonical height pairing on $E(K)$ is 
$$\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E : E(K) \times E(K) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} $$
$$\<P, Q\>_E \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E}(P+Q)-\hat{h}_{E}(P)-\hat{h}_{E}(Q) \right).$$
Likewise, for any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular, the canonical height pairing on $E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ is
$$\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_{E_{\Gamma}} : E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)) \times E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} $$
$$\<P_{\Gamma}, Q_{\Gamma}\>_{E_{\Gamma}} \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(P_{\Gamma}+Q_{\Gamma})-\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(P_{\Gamma})-\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(Q_{\Gamma}) \right).$$
It is a standard result that these pairings are bilinear on the corresponding abelian groups. However, it is more subtle when it comes to positive definiteness on the free part of the abelian group. In general, $\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E$ is positive definite on the quotient of $E(K)$ by the subgroup generated by $E(K)_\text{tors}$ and  $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\text{-trace of }E(K)$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4). Since we assume that the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is zero, it follows that $\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E$ is a positive definite bilinear form on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$. Let $P^1, \ldots, P^r$ be a set of generators for the free part of $E(K)$. The positive definiteness of the canonical height pairing on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$ implies that
$$ \det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0.$$ Let $B_E$ be the union of all $B_{P^i}$'s as in Theorem A, then $B_E$ is a finite set of codimension-two subvarieties such that for any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$ that does not contain any subvariety in $B_E$ and is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ (so that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular), then the equality in Theorem A holds for $P^1, \ldots, P^r$. By multilinearity of determinant, we have
\begin{align*}   \frac{\det \left( \<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}}{(\deg \Gamma)^r} &=\det\left( \frac{\<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma}}{\deg\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \\
&=\det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}\\
&\neq 0.
\end{align*}

On the other hand, lemma \ref{LNS} implies that there exist $N_1, \ldots, N_r$ such that the locus for which the specialization of any one of $[N_1]P^1, \ldots, [N_r]P^r$ is a singular point is of dimension at most $n-2$. So this locus contains only a finite number of subvarieties of dimension $n-2$ and we let $S_E$ be the set of all these codimension-two subvarieties. If $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\cong\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is a hyperplane such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular, we can view $E_\Gamma$ as as an elliptic curve defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$. Furthermore, if $\Gamma$ does not contain any of the subvarieties in $S_E$, then lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$ without the assumption that the reduced Weierstrass equation of $E_\Gamma$ is minimal. 



To summarize, if $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$ is a hyperplane not contained in the complement of $U$, does not contain subvarieties in $B_E \cup S_E$ and is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$, then \begin{equation}\det \left( \<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0 \end{equation} and lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$. The set of such hyperplanes $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is Zariski dense in the dual variety ${\mathbb{P}^n}^*$ (the set of hyperplanes in $\mathbb{P}^n$) because the conditions of not containing a finite number of subvarieties and not equaling any one of a certain finite number of hyperplanes are open conditions. Thus, there are infinitely many hyperplanes $\Gamma$ that allow us to reduce the dimension from $\mathbb{P}^n$ to $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$. As mentioned before, although we may not have the minimality of Weierstrass equation in the $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ case, but we do know that lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$, which is enough for Theorem A to hold true for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$ on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ and allow us to apply inductively this reduction on the dimension of the projective space and eventually reduce to the case $\mathbb{P}^2$, i.e. we may assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^2)$ with $P^1, \ldots, P^r \in E(K)$ such that $\det \left( \<P^i, P^j\>_{E} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0$. 

We continue to reduce the dimension to one as above but do not restrict ourselves to just hyperplanes, i.e. we can choose any smooth curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ of degree $d$ not contained in the complement of $U$, not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ and does not contain subvarieties in $B_E$. The union of all such curves is the Zariski open set $\mathbb{P}^2\backslash B_E$, because given any point $t \in \mathbb{P}^2(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash B_E$, we can always find a smooth curve $C/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of degree $d$ such that it contains $t$ but not points in $B_E$ and it is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ and $\mathbb{P}^2\backslash U$. With this construction, over these infinitely many curves $C$ of degree $d$, we have $\det \left( \<P^i_C, P^j_C\>_{E_C} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0$. By continuity of the determinant function and Silverman's theorem (\cite{SHS}, Theorem B), we conclude that 
$\det \left( \<{P^i_C}_t, {P^j_C}_t\>_{{E_C}_t} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0,$ for all $t \in C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with large enough $h_C(t)$. This means that the specialized points ${P^1_C}_t, \ldots, {P^r_C}_t$ are $\mathbb{Z}$-linearly independent. Since we always choose the hyperplanes (or smooth curves in the last induction step) not being contained in the complement of $U$, the specialization maps for $t \in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ commute with reduction maps as shown in Figure 1.
\begin{figure}
$$\xymatrix{
E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^n)) \ar@{->}[r]^{\sigma_t} \ar@{->}[d]_{\text{red mod $\Gamma$}} 
&E_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})  \\
E_\Gamma((\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))) \ar@{->}[d] & \\
\vdots \ar@{->}[d]_{\text{red mod $C$}} & \\
E_C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(C)) \ar@{->}[uuur]_{\sigma_t} 
}$$
\caption{}
\end{figure}
So for $t \in C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \cap U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with $h_C(t)$ large enough, we have injectivity of $\sigma_t$ on both the free part and the torsion points of $E(K)$. 

Lastly, we will prove by induction on $n$ that the union of all such curves in Theorem B is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^n$. We have just shown in the previous paragraph that the case $n=2$ is true. For $E/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^n)$ in general with $n \geq 2$, we have shown that the set of hyperplanes $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ such that condition $(\ref{LIG})$ holds on $E_\Gamma/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma\cong \mathbb{P}^{n-1})$ is Zariski dense in ${\mathbb{P}^n}^*$, thus the union of all such $\Gamma$ (call them good $\Gamma$) is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^n$. By induction hypothesis, the union of curves satisfying Theorem B for $E_\Gamma/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma\cong \mathbb{P}^{n-1})$ (call them good curves of degree $d$ for $\Gamma$) is Zariski dense in $\Gamma$. So the union 
$$ \bigcup_{\text{good $\Gamma$}} \text{union of good curves of degree $d$ for $\Gamma$}$$ is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Split on the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace; in the trace-zero case, Theorem A preserves the non-vanishing height regulator on generic hyperplane sections, inducting down to curves. Silverman's theorem then gives independence of specializations for large height.

nodes.name: Non-vanishing regulator on Gamma (LIG)
nodes.statement: \det \left( \<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0
nodes.label: LIG

nodes.name: Codimension of indeterminacy
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is a rational map between smooth projective varieties, the indeterminacy locus $I_f$ has codimension at least $2$, i.e. each irreducible component of $I_f$ has dimension at most $n-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $I_f$ has codimension $\ge 2$.

nodes.name: Restricted varieties and diagram
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $U^o$, $\Gamma^o$ and the commutative diagram of inclusions.

nodes.name: Pic isomorphisms
nodes.statement:
Since $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_f$, the codimension of $I_f \cap \Gamma$ in $\Gamma$ is at least $2$ also. Thus, we have the following isomorphisms of divisor class groups induced by $j_{\Gamma^o}$ and $j_{U^o}$:
\begin{align*} j^*_{U^o}: \operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb{P}^n) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(U^o)  &j^*_{\Gamma^o}: \operatorname{Pic}(\Gamma) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(\Gamma^o)\\
 c &\longmapsto c \cap U^o & D &\longmapsto D \cap \Gamma^o,
\end{align*} with projective closure in the corresponding varieties as the inverse maps.
nodes.statement_short: Hypothesis gives codim $\ge2$ in $\Gamma$, so restrictions induce Pic isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Diagram of class groups
nodes.statement_short: Assemble the commutative diagram of divisor class groups.

nodes.name: Functoriality and conclusion
nodes.statement:
Pull-backs are functorial on the category of varieties (\cite{FIT} Chapter 2, Section 2.2, \cite{HAG} Appendix A, Theorem 1.1), so for any divisor class $c \in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb{P}^r)$, we have 
$$\iota_{\Gamma^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))=(f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\Gamma^o})^*(c). $$ Then by taking $(j_{\Gamma^o}^*)^{-1}$, the projective closure in $\Gamma$ and tracing the commutative diagram, we get
\begin{align*}
\iota_{\Gamma}^*(f^{-1}(c))&=(j_{\Gamma^o}^*)^{-1}\left(\iota_{\Gamma^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))\right) \\& = (j_{\Gamma^o}^*)^{-1}\left((f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\Gamma^o})^*(c)\right) \\ &= (f \circ \iota_\Gamma)^{-1}(c), \end{align*} which is the statement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Functoriality of pull-backs and diagram chase give the identity.

nodes.name: Factor g through f_P
nodes.statement_short: The map induced by $P_\Gamma$ factors through $f_P\circ\iota_\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Height as degree of pull-back
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 1 and Lemma 2, $h_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)=\deg\iota_\Gamma^*(f_P^{-1}(L))$.

nodes.name: Bézout
nodes.statement:
But the divisor class $\iota_\Gamma^* (f_P^{-1}(L))$ is the divisor class of the intersection of $\Gamma$ and $f_P^{-1}(L)$ (\cite{FIT} Chapter 8, Example 8.1.7 or \cite{HAG} Chapter II, Exercises 6.2). Then by B\'ezout's theorem, we get $\deg \iota_\Gamma^* (f_P^{-1}(L)) = \deg \Gamma \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)$, which gives 
$$h_{E_\Gamma}(P_\Gamma)=\deg \Gamma \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)=\deg \Gamma \cdot h_E(P) $$ by Proposition \ref{LH} again.
nodes.statement_short: Bézout gives the factor $\deg\Gamma$; Proposition 1 again identifies $h_E(P)$.

nodes.name: Doubling formula
nodes.statement:
For $E/K$ defined by the Weierstrass equation $(\ref{WE})$ with $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where $x,y,z \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[S_0,\ldots,S_n]$, the doubling formula (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, page 324) is
\begin{align}&[2]P=\notag \\*
&[2yz\left(\left(3x^2+Az^2\right)^2-2xz(2y)^2\right): \notag \\
&-\left(3x^2+Az^2\right)^3+z(2y)^2\left(8x^3+2Axz^2-Bz^3-y^2z\right): \notag \\
&8y^3z^3]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the doubling formula (4).

nodes.name: Second doubling formula
nodes.statement:
By substituting the relation $x^3=y^2z-Axz^2-Bz^3$ into the first two coordinates and then factor away the common factor $z^2$, we also have
\begin{align}&[2]P=\notag \\
&[2y\left(xy^2-3Ax^2z-9Bxz^2+A^2z^3\right): \notag \\
&4y^2\left(7y^2-6Axz-9Bz^2\right)-\left(27(y^2-Axz-Bz^2)^2+27Ax^4+9A^2x^2z^2+A^3z^4\right): \notag \\
&8y^3z]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Eliminate $x^3$ and cancel $z^2$ to get formula (5).

nodes.name: Generic case
nodes.statement: Since by assumption $t\in\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty$ such that $P_t=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is defined and is a non-singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$, so $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ cannot be both zero. It is clear that $f_{[2]P}$ is defined when both $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ are not zero.
nodes.statement_short: $y(t),z(t)$ not both zero; if both nonzero, $f_{[2]P}$ is defined.

nodes.name: Case y(t)=0
nodes.statement: When $y(t)=0$, then $3x(t)^2+A(t)z(t)^2$ is not zero or otherwise $P_t$ is a singular point on $E_t$. So formula $(\ref{D1})$ gives $([2]P)_t=[0:1:0]$, which is not a surprise as $P_t=[x(t):0:z(t)]$ is always a 2-torsion point with the given Weierstrass equation (\ref{WEt}).
nodes.statement_short: If $y(t)=0$, formula (4) gives $([2]P)_t=O$.

nodes.name: Case z(t)=0
nodes.statement: When $z(t)=0$, then $x(t)=0$ and $y(t) \neq 0$, since $P_t$ is a point on $E_t$. Formula $(\ref{D2})$ gives $([2]P)_t=[0:y(t)^4:0]=[0:1:0]$. Thus the induced rational map $f_{[2]P}$ is defined at such $t$.
nodes.statement_short: If $z(t)=0$, formula (5) gives $([2]P)_t=O$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Lastly, formulae $(\ref{D1})$ and $(\ref{D2})$ are the same (with $A,B$ replaced by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$) doubling formula on the cubic curve $E_t$, so $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Both formulas are the doubling law on $E_t$, so $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.

nodes.name: Local ring setup
nodes.statement: For any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma$, its local ring ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ is a DVR with fraction field $K$ and residue field $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$, which is a perfect field.
nodes.statement_short: ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ is a DVR with perfect residue field.

nodes.name: Néron model and finite index
nodes.statement: With the minimality assumption on the Weierstrass equation, $E/K$ is defined by a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in ${\mathcal O}_\Gamma$ and minimal with respect to the prime divisor $\Gamma$. Thus, the smooth part of the Weierstrass model gives the N\'eron model of $E/K$ and the quotient group $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, Corollary 9.2d). So there exists $n_\Gamma \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $([n_\Gamma]P)_\Gamma$ is not a singular point on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives the Néron model, so $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite and some $n_\Gamma$ works.

nodes.name: Finitely many bad hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: Since $E_\Gamma/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$ is singular if and only if $\Gamma$ is a component of the discriminant locus and there are only finitely many such components $\Gamma_1, \ldots, \Gamma_\ell$. So $N:=\operatorname{lcm}\{n_{\Gamma_1}, \dots, n_{\Gamma_\ell}\}$ will satisfy the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Only finitely many discriminant components; take the lcm of the $n_\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Indeterminacy criterion and P'
nodes.statement: If we write $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where the homogeneous polynomials $x,y,z \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[S_0, \ldots, S_n]$ have no common irreducible factor, then the induced rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ if and only if $x(t)=y(t)=z(t)=0$, because $f_P$ maps from $\mathbb{P}^n$ and so there's no way to alter it. The corresponding point $P'$ is $[S_0^{2k}S_1^kx: S_0^{3k}y: S_1^{3k}z]$. Since at least one of $x,y,z$ has no $S_0$ as its factor, we consider all possible cases:
nodes.statement_short: $f_P$ is undefined iff $x,y,z$ vanish at $t$; write $P'$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: Case 1: $z$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. Then the only possible irreducible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx$, $S_0^{3k}y$, $S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_1$ and even if we factor out this common factor, the induced rational map $f_{P'}$ is still not defined at $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*]$.
nodes.statement_short: If $S_0\nmid z$, $f_{P'}$ is still undefined at $t$.

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: Case 2: $y$  doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. In this case, the only possible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ are $S_1$ and $S_0$. After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$. Since $y(t)=0$ and the only possible factor we factor away from $y$ in $ S_0^{3k}y$ is $S_1$, thus $y''(t)=0$. Also, $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ by assumption. If $P'_t$ is well-defined, then it is a point on the cubic curve $E_t'(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with zero $Y$-coordinate, which implies $P'_t$ is either a singular point or a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.
nodes.statement_short: If $S_0\nmid y$, $y''(t)=0$ so $P'_t$ is singular or 2-torsion.

nodes.name: Case 3
nodes.statement: Case 3: $x$  doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. The highest power of $S_0$ that can be a common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_0^{2k}$.  After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$, then we see that $y''$ always has $S_0^k$ as a factor. Thus $y''(t)=0$ and the argument follows as Case 2.
nodes.statement_short: If $S_0\nmid x$, $y''$ is divisible by $S_0^k$, reducing to Case 2.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: Now, we put ourselves in the setting described in Section \ref{lemma}. From Lemma \ref{leh}, if $\Gamma$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^m]P}$ for infinitely many $m$, then equality (\ref{E1}) holds for these $[2^m]P$ and thus dividing equation (\ref{E1}) by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the  limit $m\rightarrow \infty$ over all $m$ such that equality (\ref{E1}) holds will give us the equality in Theorem A. A priori, such $\Gamma$ might have to avoid containing infinitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\mathbb{P}^n$ corresponding to the infinitely many rational maps $f_{[2^m]P}$, we will prove that this is not a problem. In fact, we will prove that besides finitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that might be common components of the indeterminacy locus of all $f_{[2^m]P}$, $m \in \mathbb{N}$, other  codimension-two components of the indeterminacy locus of a particular $f_{[2^m]P}$ will never reappear as components of the indeterminacy locus of  $f_{[2^\ell]P}$ for any $\ell > m$.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: apply Lemma 3 to $[2^m]P$ and show the codim-2 indeterminacy components do not recur.

nodes.name: Reduce to non-singular reductions
nodes.statement: Since the canonical height is a quadratic form, we may replace $P$ by $[N]P$ in Theorem A. Given any $P \in E(K)$, we replace $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $\ref{LNS}$ to assure that $P_\Gamma$ is not a singular point of $E_\Gamma$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$. So if we let $S_P$ be the set of all $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that the specialized point $P_t$ is a singular point on the specialized fiber $E_t$, then $S_P$ is an algebraic set (since singularity is an algebraic property) of codimension at least two in $\mathbb{P}^n\backslash H_\infty$. In addition, we note that $S_P$ is contained in the discriminant locus $\Delta_E=0$. Similarly, we may assume the same for the corresponding point $P'$ on the isomorphic curve $E'$ defined by equation $(\ref{WE'})$, i.e. $P'_\Gamma$ is not a singular point of $E'_\Gamma$  for all smooth hypersurfaces $\Gamma \neq H'_\infty$ and $S_{P'}$ has codimension at least $2$ in $\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $P$ by $[N]P$ via Lemma 5 so that the singular locus $S_P$ has codim $\ge 2$; same for $P'$.

nodes.name: Indeterminacy away from H_infinity
nodes.statement: As before, let $I_{f_P}$ be the indeterminacy locus of the rational map $f_P$ induced by $P$. Then for all $t \in \mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ that are not in $I_{f_P} \cup S_P$, $f_P(t)=P_t$ is well-defined and is not a singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$. By lemma \ref{DL} and induction on $m$, $f_{[2^m]P}(t)=\left( [2^m]P\right)_t=[2^m]P_t$ is well-defined for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Thus, $$I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap \left(\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \right) \subset I_{f_P}\cup S_P, \qquad\text{ for all }m \in \mathbb{N}.$$
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 4 and induction on $m$, $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ off $H_\infty$ lies in $I_{f_P}\cup S_P$.

nodes.name: Points on H_infinity do not recur
nodes.statement:
For $$t=[0:1:*: \dots:*] \in \left(I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\right) \backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}),$$ if $t \not \in  I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}$, then lemma \ref{DL} says that $f_{[2^m]P'}(t)=([2^m]P')_t$ is defined and non-singular on $E'_t$ because $([2^m]P')_t=[2^m]P'_t$. In particular, lemma \ref{PL} implies that in fact $[2^m]P'$ is a point of order $2$ on $E'_t$. Thus, for $\ell > m$, $([2^\ell]P')_t=[2^\ell]P'_t=[2^{\ell-m}]\left([2^m]P'_t\right)=O_{E'_t}$, which implies that $t$ is not in $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ by the contrapositive statement of lemma \ref{PL}. Notice that we are left with $t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\cap H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, which is an algebraic set of codimension at least $2$ in $\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$. To summarize, we have shown that given $P\in E(K)$, by replacing $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $\ref{LNS}$ if necessary, so that $P_\Gamma$ and $P'_\Gamma$ are not singular points of $E_\Gamma$ and $E'_\Gamma$ respectively for all smooth hypersurface $\Gamma$, for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, if 
$$
  t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  t \notin I_{f_P} \cup I_{f_{P'}} \cup S_P \cup S_{P'} \cup (H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\cap H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})),
$$
then for any $\ell>m$, $t \not \in I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$. In particular, if we let
$$B_P:=\left\{ H_\infty\cap H'_\infty, \ \text{dimension-$(n-2)$ components of }I_{f_P}\cup I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_P\cup S_{P'}   \right\}, $$then for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, if $C$ is a dimension-$(n-2)$ component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ that is not in $B_P$, then $C$ is not a component of  $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ for all $\ell > m$.
nodes.statement_short: On $H_\infty\setminus H'_\infty$, Lemmas 4 and 6 show indeterminacy points of $f_{[2^m]P}$ outside $B_P$ do not recur for larger exponents.

nodes.name: 2-torsion argument
nodes.statement: For $$t=[0:1:*: \dots:*] \in \left(I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\right) \backslash H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}),$$ if $t \not \in  I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}$, then lemma \ref{DL} says that $f_{[2^m]P'}(t)=([2^m]P')_t$ is defined and non-singular on $E'_t$ because $([2^m]P')_t=[2^m]P'_t$. In particular, lemma \ref{PL} implies that in fact $[2^m]P'$ is a point of order $2$ on $E'_t$. Thus, for $\ell > m$, $([2^\ell]P')_t=[2^\ell]P'_t=[2^{\ell-m}]\left([2^m]P'_t\right)=O_{E'_t}$, which implies that $t$ is not in $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ by the contrapositive statement of lemma \ref{PL}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6 forces $[2^m]P'_t$ to be 2-torsion, so higher multiples are $O$ and $f_{[2^\ell]P}$ is defined at $t$.

nodes.name: Remaining locus
nodes.statement: Notice that we are left with $t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\cap H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, which is an algebraic set of codimension at least $2$ in $\mathbb{P}^n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.
nodes.statement_short: What remains lies in $H_\infty\cap H'_\infty$, of codim 2.

nodes.name: Summary
nodes.statement:
To summarize, we have shown that given $P\in E(K)$, by replacing $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $\ref{LNS}$ if necessary, so that $P_\Gamma$ and $P'_\Gamma$ are not singular points of $E_\Gamma$ and $E'_\Gamma$ respectively for all smooth hypersurface $\Gamma$, for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, if 
$$
  t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  t \notin I_{f_P} \cup I_{f_{P'}} \cup S_P \cup S_{P'} \cup (H_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\cap H'_\infty(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})),
$$
then for any $\ell>m$, $t \not \in I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Indeterminacy points outside the exceptional loci never recur.

nodes.name: Define B_P
nodes.statement:
In particular, if we let
$$B_P:=\left\{ H_\infty\cap H'_\infty, \ \text{dimension-$(n-2)$ components of }I_{f_P}\cup I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_P\cup S_{P'}   \right\}, $$then for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, if $C$ is a dimension-$(n-2)$ component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ that is not in $B_P$, then $C$ is not a component of  $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ for all $\ell > m$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $B_P$; codim-2 components outside $B_P$ do not recur.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: To complete the proof for Theorem A, we consider any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ that is not a component of the discriminant locus, so $E_\Gamma$ is an elliptic curve over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)$. Furthermore, if $\Gamma$ does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$, then we have just shown that $\Gamma$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ for all big enough $m \in \mathbb{N}$. So by lemma \ref{leh}, we have $$\frac{h_{E_\Gamma}([2^m]P_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}=\frac{h_{E_\Gamma}(\left([2^m]P\right)_\Gamma)}{\deg \Gamma}= h_E([2^m]P) $$ for all big enough $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Dividing this equation by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the limit $m\rightarrow \infty$ will give us Theorem A.
nodes.statement_short: For large $m$ Lemma 3 applies to $[2^m]P$; divide by $3\cdot 2^{2m}$ and take the limit.

nodes.name: Nonzero trace case
nodes.statement: If the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6) is non-zero, then by the constraint of dimension, the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is a dimensional one abelian variety, i.e. $E$ is $K$-isomorphic to $E_0 \times_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} K$ for an elliptic curve $E_0/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. So there is a Zariski dense open subset $U^0 \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ such that for all $t \in U^0(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, the fibers $E_t$ are isomorphic to $E_0$, thus the specialization maps for $\sigma_t: E_0 \times_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} K \longrightarrow E_t$  are injective for all $t \in U^0(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$. So in particular, any curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ of degree $d$ that does not lie in the complement of $U^0$ will satisfies Theorem B and their union is $\mathbb{P}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: If the trace is nonzero, $E$ is constant generically and all $\sigma_t$ are injective on an open set.

nodes.name: Zero trace case
nodes.statement:
We now suppose that the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is zero, which implies that $E(K)$ is finitely generated, a result due to Lang-N\'eron (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 2). For any non-zero $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$, the algebraic set
$$ \{ t \in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\ | \ [x(t):y(t):z(t)]=\sigma_t(P)=O=[0:1:0] \}$$ has dimension at most $n-1$. Since the subgroup of torsion points $E(K)_{\text{tors}}$ is finite, so we may shrink $U$ by discarding finitely many subvarieties of dimension at most $n-1$ and assume that 
$$E(K)_{\text{tors}} \longrightarrow E_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) $$
is injective for all $t \in  U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$. On the other hand, We will use the canonical height pairing to prove that the specialization map is injective on the free part of $E(K)$. The canonical height pairing on $E(K)$ is 
$$\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E : E(K) \times E(K) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} $$
$$\<P, Q\>_E \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E}(P+Q)-\hat{h}_{E}(P)-\hat{h}_{E}(Q) \right).$$
Likewise, for any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular, the canonical height pairing on $E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ is
$$\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_{E_{\Gamma}} : E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)) \times E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} $$
$$\<P_{\Gamma}, Q_{\Gamma}\>_{E_{\Gamma}} \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(P_{\Gamma}+Q_{\Gamma})-\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(P_{\Gamma})-\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(Q_{\Gamma}) \right).$$
It is a standard result that these pairings are bilinear on the corresponding abelian groups. However, it is more subtle when it comes to positive definiteness on the free part of the abelian group. In general, $\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E$ is positive definite on the quotient of $E(K)$ by the subgroup generated by $E(K)_\text{tors}$ and  $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\text{-trace of }E(K)$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4). Since we assume that the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is zero, it follows that $\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E$ is a positive definite bilinear form on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$. Let $P^1, \ldots, P^r$ be a set of generators for the free part of $E(K)$. The positive definiteness of the canonical height pairing on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$ implies that
$$ \det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0.$$ Let $B_E$ be the union of all $B_{P^i}$'s as in Theorem A, then $B_E$ is a finite set of codimension-two subvarieties such that for any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$ that does not contain any subvariety in $B_E$ and is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ (so that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular), then the equality in Theorem A holds for $P^1, \ldots, P^r$. By multilinearity of determinant, we have
\begin{align*}   \frac{\det \left( \<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}}{(\deg \Gamma)^r} &=\det\left( \frac{\<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma}}{\deg\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \\
&=\det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}\\
&\neq 0.
\end{align*}

On the other hand, lemma \ref{LNS} implies that there exist $N_1, \ldots, N_r$ such that the locus for which the specialization of any one of $[N_1]P^1, \ldots, [N_r]P^r$ is a singular point is of dimension at most $n-2$. So this locus contains only a finite number of subvarieties of dimension $n-2$ and we let $S_E$ be the set of all these codimension-two subvarieties. If $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\cong\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is a hyperplane such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular, we can view $E_\Gamma$ as as an elliptic curve defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$. Furthermore, if $\Gamma$ does not contain any of the subvarieties in $S_E$, then lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$ without the assumption that the reduced Weierstrass equation of $E_\Gamma$ is minimal. 



To summarize, if $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$ is a hyperplane not contained in the complement of $U$, does not contain subvarieties in $B_E \cup S_E$ and is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$, then \begin{equation}\det \left( \<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0 \end{equation} and lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$. The set of such hyperplanes $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is Zariski dense in the dual variety ${\mathbb{P}^n}^*$ (the set of hyperplanes in $\mathbb{P}^n$) because the conditions of not containing a finite number of subvarieties and not equaling any one of a certain finite number of hyperplanes are open conditions. Thus, there are infinitely many hyperplanes $\Gamma$ that allow us to reduce the dimension from $\mathbb{P}^n$ to $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$. As mentioned before, although we may not have the minimality of Weierstrass equation in the $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ case, but we do know that lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$, which is enough for Theorem A to hold true for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$ on $E_\Gamma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ and allow us to apply inductively this reduction on the dimension of the projective space and eventually reduce to the case $\mathbb{P}^2$, i.e. we may assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^2)$ with $P^1, \ldots, P^r \in E(K)$ such that $\det \left( \<P^i, P^j\>_{E} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0$. 

We continue to reduce the dimension to one as above but do not restrict ourselves to just hyperplanes, i.e. we can choose any smooth curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ of degree $d$ not contained in the complement of $U$, not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ and does not contain subvarieties in $B_E$. The union of all such curves is the Zariski open set $\mathbb{P}^2\backslash B_E$, because given any point $t \in \mathbb{P}^2(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\backslash B_E$, we can always find a smooth curve $C/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of degree $d$ such that it contains $t$ but not points in $B_E$ and it is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ and $\mathbb{P}^2\backslash U$. With this construction, over these infinitely many curves $C$ of degree $d$, we have $\det \left( \<P^i_C, P^j_C\>_{E_C} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0$. By continuity of the determinant function and Silverman's theorem (\cite{SHS}, Theorem B), we conclude that 
$\det \left( \<{P^i_C}_t, {P^j_C}_t\>_{{E_C}_t} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0,$ for all $t \in C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with large enough $h_C(t)$. This means that the specialized points ${P^1_C}_t, \ldots, {P^r_C}_t$ are $\mathbb{Z}$-linearly independent. Since we always choose the hyperplanes (or smooth curves in the last induction step) not being contained in the complement of $U$, the specialization maps for $t \in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ commute with reduction maps as shown in Figure 1.
\begin{figure}
$$\xymatrix{
E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^n)) \ar@{->}[r]^{\sigma_t} \ar@{->}[d]_{\text{red mod $\Gamma$}} 
&E_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})  \\
E_\Gamma((\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))) \ar@{->}[d] & \\
\vdots \ar@{->}[d]_{\text{red mod $C$}} & \\
E_C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(C)) \ar@{->}[uuur]_{\sigma_t} 
}$$
\caption{}
\end{figure}
So for $t \in C(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \cap U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with $h_C(t)$ large enough, we have injectivity of $\sigma_t$ on both the free part and the torsion points of $E(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: If the trace is zero, $E(K)$ is finitely generated; show torsion and free parts specialize injectively on suitable curves.

nodes.name: Torsion injectivity
nodes.statement:
We now suppose that the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is zero, which implies that $E(K)$ is finitely generated, a result due to Lang-N\'eron (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 2). For any non-zero $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$, the algebraic set
$$ \{ t \in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\ | \ [x(t):y(t):z(t)]=\sigma_t(P)=O=[0:1:0] \}$$ has dimension at most $n-1$. Since the subgroup of torsion points $E(K)_{\text{tors}}$ is finite, so we may shrink $U$ by discarding finitely many subvarieties of dimension at most $n-1$ and assume that 
$$E(K)_{\text{tors}} \longrightarrow E_t(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) $$
is injective for all $t \in  U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Lang-Néron: $E(K)$ finitely generated; shrinking $U$ makes torsion specialize injectively.

nodes.name: Canonical height pairings
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, We will use the canonical height pairing to prove that the specialization map is injective on the free part of $E(K)$. The canonical height pairing on $E(K)$ is 
$$\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E : E(K) \times E(K) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} $$
$$\<P, Q\>_E \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E}(P+Q)-\hat{h}_{E}(P)-\hat{h}_{E}(Q) \right).$$
Likewise, for any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular, the canonical height pairing on $E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma))$ is
$$\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_{E_{\Gamma}} : E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)) \times E_{\Gamma}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\Gamma)) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} $$
$$\<P_{\Gamma}, Q_{\Gamma}\>_{E_{\Gamma}} \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(P_{\Gamma}+Q_{\Gamma})-\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(P_{\Gamma})-\hat{h}_{E_{\Gamma}}(Q_{\Gamma}) \right).$$
It is a standard result that these pairings are bilinear on the corresponding abelian groups.
nodes.statement_short: Define the canonical height pairings on $E(K)$ and $E_\Gamma$; they are bilinear.

nodes.name: Nonzero regulator
nodes.statement:
However, it is more subtle when it comes to positive definiteness on the free part of the abelian group. In general, $\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E$ is positive definite on the quotient of $E(K)$ by the subgroup generated by $E(K)_\text{tors}$ and  $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\text{-trace of }E(K)$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4). Since we assume that the $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-trace of $E$ is zero, it follows that $\< \cdot  , \cdot \>_E$ is a positive definite bilinear form on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$. Let $P^1, \ldots, P^r$ be a set of generators for the free part of $E(K)$. The positive definiteness of the canonical height pairing on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$ implies that
$$ \det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Positive definiteness (Lang) gives a nonzero regulator for generators $P^1,\dots,P^r$.

nodes.name: Regulator survives on Gamma
nodes.statement:
Let $B_E$ be the union of all $B_{P^i}$'s as in Theorem A, then $B_E$ is a finite set of codimension-two subvarieties such that for any smooth hypersurface $\Gamma \neq H_\infty$ that does not contain any subvariety in $B_E$ and is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ (so that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular), then the equality in Theorem A holds for $P^1, \ldots, P^r$. By multilinearity of determinant, we have
\begin{align*}   \frac{\det \left( \<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}}{(\deg \Gamma)^r} &=\det\left( \frac{\<P^i_\Gamma, P^j_\Gamma\>_{E_\Gamma}}{\deg\Gamma} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \\
&=\det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}\\
&\neq 0.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Theorem A for each generator and multilinearity give a nonzero regulator over $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Singular-reduction locus S_E
nodes.statement: On the other hand, lemma \ref{LNS} implies that there exist $N_1, \ldots, N_r$ such that the locus for which the specialization of any one of $[N_1]P^1, \ldots, [N_r]P^r$ is a singular point is of dimension at most $n-2$. So this locus contains only a finite number of subvarieties of dimension $n-2$ and we let $S_E$ be the set of all these codimension-two subvarieties. If $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\cong\Gamma \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is a hyperplane such that $E_\Gamma$ is non-singular, we can view $E_\Gamma$ as as an elliptic curve defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$. Furthermore, if $\Gamma$ does not contain any of the subvarieties in $S_E$, then lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\Gamma, \ldots, P^r_\Gamma$ without the assumption that the reduced Weierstrass equation of $E_\Gamma$ is minimal.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 5 the singular-specialization locus is finite in codim 2; hyperplanes avoiding it keep Lemma 5 valid.

nodes.name: Induct down to P^2
nodes.statement_short: Good hyperplanes are Zariski dense; iterate the reduction down to $\mathbb{P}^2$.

nodes.name: Curves and Silverman's theorem
nodes.statement_short: On smooth degree-$d$ curves the regulator stays nonzero; Silverman's theorem gives independence of specializations for large $h_C(t)$.

nodes.name: Zariski density by induction
nodes.statement: Lastly, we will prove by induction on $n$ that the union of all such curves in Theorem B is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $n$: good hyperplanes are dense and good curves are dense in each.
